cards.heading: Three-tier campus
cards.body: A large campus uses three layers. Access connects endpoints (PoE, port security, VLANs). Distribution aggregates access switches, routes between VLANs and applies policy. Core is a fast, highly available backbone between distribution blocks.

Core   ═══   Core
       /    \       /    \
   Dist      Dist  Dist      Dist
   / | \                 / | \
 Access switches       Access switches

cards.heading: Two-tier (collapsed core)
cards.body: Smaller campuses merge core and distribution into one layer: the collapsed core. It saves cost when a separate core layer wouldn't add anything.

cards.heading: Spine-leaf
cards.body: Data centres use spine-leaf: every leaf switch connects to every spine switch, and spines don't connect to each other, nor do leaves. Any server is the same number of hops (leaf-spine-leaf) from any other, which suits east-west traffic between servers. Grow by adding leaves (ports) or spines (bandwidth). Traffic between servers on two different leaves always passes through three switches: leaf, spine, leaf.

cards.heading: WAN
cards.body: A wide area network links sites over large distances, usually with a service provider: leased lines, MPLS, metro Ethernet, or VPNs over the internet. Topologies include point-to-point, hub-and-spoke and full or partial mesh. In hub-and-spoke, branches connect only to the central hub, so branch-to-branch traffic passes through the hub. A full mesh links every site directly, so there is no single hub to fail, but it needs n(n-1)/2 links, which gets expensive.

cards.heading: SOHO
cards.body: A small office/home office often uses one device that combines a router, switch, firewall and wireless AP, with a single internet connection.

cards.heading: On-premises and cloud
cards.body: On-premises means you own and run the equipment in your own building. Cloud means the provider runs it and you pay for what you use. The main models are IaaS (infrastructure: VMs and networks), PaaS (a platform to run your code) and SaaS (finished applications such as webmail). Public, private and hybrid clouds differ in who shares the resources.
